title: India Parliament opens review of Digital India Act generative-AI liability clauses
subtitle: The revised bill removes intermediary safe harbor for generative-AI outputs that cause documented economic harm or produce deepfakes of public figures.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The Indian Parliament began formal review on September 21 of the Digital India Act's generative-AI liability clauses. The revised bill introduces a statutory strict-liability framework and — for the first time in Indian law — removes the intermediary safe-harbor shield when generative-AI outputs cause documented economic harm or disseminate deepfakes of public figures. If enacted, deployers and platform operators become directly answerable for those outputs, not merely for takedown compliance.

The clauses build on India's February notification of the amended IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, which took effect on February 20 and had already tightened labeling and provenance duties for synthetic media. The Digital India Act goes further by codifying strict liability at the statute level — a legal standard that does not require proof of intent or negligence, only that the harm occurred and the AI system produced it.

The move puts India near the strict end of the current global spectrum. The EU's AI Act relies on tiered risk classes with human-oversight duties; the US so far has state-level patchwork; China's rules are enforcement-heavy but concentrated on content control. A statutory strict-liability regime targeting economic harm and deepfakes of public figures is closer to product-liability law than to the platform-liability posture most jurisdictions still use, and multinational deployers will need to model India separately in their compliance stacks.

A note for learners: strict liability changes engineering economics, not just legal risk. Under a negligence standard, a lab can defend its release by showing reasonable care; under strict liability, the question is whether the harm happened. That pushes cost into pre-deployment evaluation, provenance tracking, and refusal training — capabilities students and early-career engineers will increasingly see on job descriptions as this regulatory shape spreads.
